title: What the Early Church Believed About Life After Death
question: What did the first Christians believe happens when you die, and how did they think it would all end?
plainAnswer: The earliest Christians did not mainly hope for their souls to float off to heaven forever. Their great hope was the resurrection: on the last day God would raise the dead bodily, as he had raised Jesus, and renew the world. In between death and resurrection, most believed the dead wait in a conscious 'holding' state, called Hades, paradise or Abraham's bosom, with martyrs often thought to go straight to Christ. They believed Christ himself had gone down to the realm of the dead, they prayed for and remembered the departed, and they argued hard with Greek thinkers who prized the soul but despised the body. Over time the two ideas, an immortal soul and a raised body, were woven together into the classic Christian picture.
keyTakeaways: The central early hope was bodily resurrection on the last day, not the soul's escape from the body.
Most early writers taught an 'intermediate state': the dead are conscious and waiting, not yet in their final condition.
Martyrs were widely believed to enter Christ's presence at once, which gave their deaths huge meaning for the churches.
Christ's descent to the dead (later called the 'harrowing of hell') is attested early, in the second century, not first in the Middle Ages.
Christians prayed for and remembered the dead from at least about AD 200, though this did not yet mean the later doctrine of purgatory.
Greek ideas of the soul's immortality were both resisted and borrowed; the result was a synthesis, not a simple takeover.

sections.heading: The starting point: Jewish hope and Jesus' resurrection
sections.body:
Christianity was born inside a Judaism that was divided about the afterlife. The older scriptures mostly picture the dead going down to Sheol, a shadowy place of silence (Ps 6:5, Eccl 9:10). Later texts speak of a coming day when 'many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake' (Dan 12:2). By Jesus' time Pharisees affirmed resurrection, while Sadducees denied it (Acts 23:6-8, Matt 22:23-32).

The first Christians took the Pharisees' side, but with a twist nobody expected. They claimed that one man, Jesus, had already been raised ahead of everyone else, as the 'firstfruits' of a coming harvest (1 Cor 15:20-23). Resurrection was not just a future doctrine; it had started.

This is why early Christian hope looked forward to a body, not away from one. Paul says the resurrection body will be different, 'spiritual' and imperishable, but still a body (1 Cor 15:42-44). His hope is not to be 'unclothed' but 'further clothed' (2 Cor 5:1-4), and he expects Christ to transform 'our lowly body' to be like his glorious body (Phil 3:20-21).

sources.author: N. T. Wright
sources.title: The Resurrection of the Son of God

sources.author: Brian E. Daley
sources.title: The Hope of the Early Church: A Handbook of Patristic Eschatology

callout.text: Myth: 'Early Christians believed that when you die your soul goes to heaven, and that is the final goal.' Correction: for the earliest writers, going to be 'with Christ' at death (Phil 1:23) was real but temporary. The goal was resurrection and a renewed creation. The creeds confess 'the resurrection of the body' (Apostles' Creed) and 'the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come' (Nicene Creed, 381), not simply 'the soul going to heaven'.

sections.heading: Resurrection of the flesh: why the body mattered so much
sections.body:
In the second century, Christians had to defend bodily resurrection on two fronts. Pagan critics found it disgusting or absurd: why would anyone want a corpse back? Some Christian groups, often called Gnostics, agreed with the critics and taught that only the spirit is saved.

Mainstream writers answered firmly. Clement of Rome (around AD 96) points to day and night and seeds rising from the earth as pictures of resurrection. Justin Martyr argues that the God who formed a human from a tiny seed can certainly raise a body again. The Martyrdom of Polycarp has the old bishop praying to share in 'the resurrection to eternal life, both of soul and body.' Irenaeus of Lyon devotes much of book five of *Against Heresies* to the claim that the flesh, which God made and Christ took on, is capable of salvation. Tertullian wrote a whole treatise titled *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*, around 208.

The point was not only about the future. If God would raise the body, then the body is good, creation is good, and what Christians did with their bodies mattered now. That is how the early writers connected the resurrection with sexual ethics, care for the poor and sick, and burial of the dead.

sources.author: Tertullian
sources.title: On the Resurrection of the Flesh

sources.author: Caroline Walker Bynum
sources.title: The Resurrection of the Body in Western Christianity, 200-1336

callout.text: When Paul preached the resurrection in Athens, some listeners mocked (Acts 17:32). The second-century pagan Celsus later called the Christian hope a 'hope of worms', according to Origen's reply *Against Celsus* (book 5; exact section needs verification). Bodily resurrection was the most offensive part of the message to educated Greeks, not a borrowed Greek idea.

sections.heading: Between death and resurrection: Hades, paradise and Abraham's bosom
sections.body:
If the resurrection comes only on the last day, where are the dead now? The New Testament gives glimpses rather than a map. Jesus tells of a poor man carried to 'Abraham's bosom' while a rich man suffers in Hades, with a great gulf between them (Luke 16:19-31). He promises the dying thief, 'today you will be with me in paradise' (Luke 23:43). Paul speaks of departing to 'be with Christ' (Phil 1:23) and being 'at home with the Lord' (2 Cor 5:8). Revelation shows martyrs' souls under the heavenly altar, crying out and told to wait (Rev 6:9-11).

Most second- and third-century writers drew a picture from these texts: at death the soul goes to a place of waiting, often called Hades in the broad sense of 'the realm of the dead'. It is divided, with the righteous at rest and the wicked already in distress. Final reward and final punishment both wait for the resurrection and judgment. Irenaeus says souls go to an invisible place appointed by God and remain there until the resurrection. Tertullian, in *On the Soul*, describes all souls as held in the underworld until the last day, with the exception of the martyrs.

Justin Martyr even warned against people who say there is no resurrection and that souls are taken up to heaven at death, saying such people should not be counted as Christians. For him, skipping straight to heaven was a sign of denying the resurrection.

This 'intermediate state' teaching was not uniform. Some later writers, especially in the fourth century, spoke of the righteous being with Christ in heaven already, and the question of whether the saints see God before the resurrection was argued about for centuries (it was settled for Roman Catholics by *Benedictus Deus* in 1336).

sources.author: Brian E. Daley
sources.title: The Hope of the Early Church: A Handbook of Patristic Eschatology

callout.text: Christians still debate what Luke 16 teaches. Some read the story of the rich man and Lazarus as a window into the intermediate state. Others treat it as a parable using familiar Jewish imagery to make a moral point about wealth and repentance, not a literal description. Both readings are old.

sections.heading: The martyrs: straight to Christ
sections.body:
One group was treated differently from the start: the martyrs. Revelation pictures those 'slain for the word of God' as already before God's altar (Rev 6:9-11), and Stephen, the first martyr, sees heaven opened and commits his spirit to Jesus as he dies (Acts 7:55-60).

Tertullian says plainly that while ordinary souls wait in the underworld, the martyrs go directly to paradise. Their deaths were described as a 'birthday' into true life. The Martyrdom of Polycarp, written soon after his death around 155, says the church at Smyrna gathered his bones and planned to meet each year on the day of his martyrdom to remember him and prepare others for their own trials. This is one of the earliest witnesses to the Christian cult of the saints.

The martyrs mattered because they made the resurrection hope visible. A person who died singing, rather than cursing, was public evidence that Christians really believed death had lost its sting (1 Cor 15:55). Over the following centuries, martyrs' tombs became places of prayer, and asking the martyrs to pray for the living became widespread.

sources.author: Peter Brown
sources.title: The Cult of the Saints: Its Rise and Function in Latin Christianity

callout.text: The practice of gathering at martyrs' tombs on the anniversary of their deaths is extra-biblical church tradition. It is attested by the mid-second century and grew into the calendar of saints' days.

sections.heading: Christ's descent to the dead
sections.body:
Early Christians believed that between his death and resurrection Jesus went to the realm of the dead. Peter's sermon applies Psalm 16 to Jesus: God did not abandon him to Hades (Acts 2:27, Acts 2:31). Jesus speaks of the Son of Man being 'three days and three nights in the heart of the earth' (Matt 12:40). Two hard passages in 1 Peter speak of Christ preaching 'to the spirits in prison' and the gospel being preached 'to the dead' (1 Pet 3:18-20, 1 Pet 4:6). Ephesians says he 'descended into the lower parts of the earth' (Eph 4:8-10).

By the early second century, Ignatius of Antioch says the prophets, who were Christ's disciples in the Spirit, were raised by him when he came. Justin and Irenaeus both cite a saying they attribute to Jeremiah (it is not in our book of Jeremiah) about the Lord remembering his dead and going down to preach salvation to them. Later, the *Gospel of Nicodemus* told the story dramatically: Christ smashes the gates of Hades and leads out Adam, Eve and the righteous of old. This became the 'harrowing of hell' of medieval art and the central Easter icon of Eastern Orthodoxy.

The phrase 'he descended into hell' entered some Western creeds in the fourth century and became part of the Apostles' Creed. What it means has been debated. Some say Christ proclaimed victory, others that he freed Old Testament saints, others (following Calvin) that it describes his spiritual anguish on the cross, and some modern evangelicals (such as Wayne Grudem) argue the line should be dropped.

sources.author: Anonymous
sources.title: Gospel of Nicodemus (Acts of Pilate), Descent into Hell

sources.author: Wayne Grudem
sources.title: He Did Not Descend into Hell: A Plea for Following Scripture instead of the Apostles' Creed

callout.text: Myth: 'The descent into hell is a late medieval invention.' Correction: the idea is attested by Ignatius (about 110) and Irenaeus (about 180). What came later was the dramatic storytelling and the creedal wording. What is genuinely debated is what 1 Peter 3:19 means, not whether early Christians believed in a descent.

sections.heading: Prayers and offerings for the dead
sections.body:
Christians did not stop loving the dead, and from early on they prayed for them. Around 200, Tertullian mentions offerings made for the dead on the anniversaries of their deaths as an accepted custom, and he urges a widow to pray for her late husband's soul. In the *Passion of Perpetua and Felicity* (203), Perpetua prays for her dead little brother Dinocrates and sees in a vision that his suffering is relieved. Christian tomb inscriptions in Rome ask for peace and refreshment for the departed. Augustine, in his *Confessions*, asks readers to remember his mother Monica at the altar.

The New Testament does not command prayer for the dead. Supporters point to Paul's wish that the Lord grant mercy to Onesiphorus 'on that day' (2 Tim 1:16-18), which some read as a prayer for a man who had died. Jewish precedent is often cited from 2 Maccabees 12, where Judas Maccabeus makes an offering for fallen soldiers; Protestants do not accept 2 Maccabees as scripture, while Catholics and Orthodox do.

These early prayers asked for rest, light, peace and mercy. They did not yet assume a fully worked-out doctrine of purgatory as a place of cleansing with set durations. That doctrine developed slowly in the West, with major steps in Augustine and Gregory the Great and formal definition at the councils of Lyon (1274), Florence (1439) and Trent (1563). The Orthodox Church prays for the dead but does not accept the Western definition of purgatory, and Protestant Reformers rejected both purgatory and prayers for the dead.

sources.author: Anonymous (with Perpetua's own account)
sources.title: The Passion of Perpetua and Felicity

callout.text: Myth (from two directions): 'Prayer for the dead proves the early church believed in purgatory', or 'prayer for the dead was a medieval corruption.' Correction: prayer for the dead is early, about AD 200 at the latest. Purgatory as later defined is a later development built partly on that practice. Both the continuity and the development are real.

sections.heading: Greek immortality and Christian resurrection: clash and synthesis
sections.body:
Many educated Greeks, following Plato's *Phaedo*, believed the soul is immortal by nature, existed before birth, and is freed at death from the prison of the body. Early Christians reacted in different ways.

Some resisted the idea that the soul is naturally immortal. Theophilus of Antioch said humans were made neither mortal nor immortal by nature, but capable of either. Tatian argued the soul is not immortal in itself but can die and rise. Justin and Irenaeus said souls exist only as long as God wills. Christian writers also flatly rejected the pre-existence of souls and reincarnation.

Others found Platonic language helpful for saying that the person survives death and is accountable to God. Origen of Alexandria (died about 253) drew deeply on Platonist philosophy and taught the pre-existence of souls, which later got his followers condemned. By the fourth and fifth centuries, writers like Gregory of Nyssa and Augustine held both that the soul survives death by God's design and that the body will be raised. Medieval theology (for example Thomas Aquinas) completed this synthesis: the soul is the 'form' of the body, can exist without it after death, but is incomplete until the resurrection.

Scholars disagree about how to judge this. Some (for example Oscar Cullmann) argued that 'immortality of the soul' and 'resurrection of the dead' are basically opposed ideas, and that the church drifted from the second to the first. Others (for example John W. Cooper) argue that scripture itself implies a soul that survives death, so the synthesis was faithful. Many historians take a middle view: the church borrowed vocabulary but kept resurrection as the final hope.

sources.author: Oscar Cullmann
sources.title: Immortality of the Soul or Resurrection of the Dead?

callout.text: Myth: 'Christians simply copied the immortal soul from Plato.' Correction: early Christians rejected key Platonic beliefs (pre-existence, reincarnation, the body as a prison) and insisted on bodily resurrection, which Platonists found absurd. Some vocabulary was borrowed, and how far that changed the substance is a genuine debate.

sections.heading: Judgment, punishment and other open questions
sections.body:
The early church agreed that Christ would return to judge the living and the dead (2 Tim 4:1, Acts 10:42). Most writers, from 2 Clement and Justin to Augustine, taught that the wicked would suffer eternal punishment. A minority hoped that punishment would be corrective and that all would finally be restored (Origen, Gregory of Nyssa). Some writers have been read as conditionalists, who thought the wicked would finally cease to exist; how strongly to read them is debated. These three views are explained in the guide 'Heaven and Hell Explained'.

Many early Christians also expected an earthly thousand-year reign of Christ before the final new creation (Papias, Justin, Irenaeus), a view called chiliasm that later faded in the East and was reinterpreted by Augustine in the West. See the guide 'The Future of the Earth'.

The overall picture is of a church with a firm centre (Christ is risen, the dead will be raised, God will judge and renew all things) and a wide fringe of open questions that were argued about openly, sometimes for centuries.

views.name: Resurrection-centred (earliest emphasis)
views.summary: The dead wait; the real goal is the raising of the body and renewal of the world. Strong in Justin, Irenaeus and Tertullian; recovered today by writers like N. T. Wright.

views.name: Classic synthesis
views.summary: The soul survives death by God's design and may already enjoy God's presence, but is incomplete until resurrection. Developed by Augustine and Aquinas; held by Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant confessions.

views.name: Soul-sleep or mortalist
views.summary: The dead are unconscious until the resurrection. Held by some early writers on a debated reading, by some Reformation-era radicals, and today by Seventh-day Adventists and some others.

Is the story of the rich man and Lazarus a description of the afterlife or a parable with a moral point?
What did Peter mean by Christ preaching to 'the spirits in prison'?
Did borrowing Greek ideas about the soul enrich Christian hope or distort it?
Why did the martyrs become so important to the early churches?

title: The Future of the Earth
question: Did the early Christians expect to leave the earth behind for heaven, or for God to renew the earth itself?
plainAnswer: Most early Christians expected the earth to be renewed, not thrown away. Paul says creation itself is 'groaning' and will be set free (Rom 8:19-23), and Revelation ends with a new heaven and new earth and God coming to live with people (Rev 21:1-5). Many second-century leaders, such as Papias, Justin and Irenaeus, even expected a literal thousand-year reign of Christ on a restored earth. That expectation faded after Origen and Augustine, and over the Middle Ages and later, popular piety focused more on the soul 'going to heaven'. In the last few decades many scholars, such as N. T. Wright and J. Richard Middleton, have argued for recovering the 'renewed earth' hope, while others warn against losing the older focus on seeing God himself.
keyTakeaways: The Bible speaks of a 'new heaven and new earth' (Isa 65:17, Rev 21:1), and most early writers read this as renewal rather than replacement.
2 Peter 3 speaks of fire and dissolution, but it also has a famous textual question (is the earth 'burned up' or 'laid bare'?), and it ends with a new heaven and earth.
Chiliasm, the hope of a thousand-year earthly kingdom, was widespread in the second century and championed by Irenaeus.
Origen and later Augustine moved the church away from literal chiliasm, and the hope became more spiritual and heavenly in tone.
'Going to heaven when you die' as the whole goal is largely a later, popular emphasis, though medieval theology never fully dropped resurrection.
Modern 'new creation' writers have critics who say they downplay the vision of God and overstate the contrast with tradition.

sections.heading: The Old Testament promise: a renewed world
sections.body:
The story of the Bible begins with God calling creation 'very good' (Gen 1:31). The prophets do not look forward to leaving it. Isaiah promises 'new heavens and a new earth' where Jerusalem is a joy, people build houses and live in them, plant vineyards and eat their fruit, and 'the wolf and the lamb shall feed together' (Isa 65:17-25). This is a picture of ordinary life healed, not abolished.

Other prophetic texts share the same earthy hope: the earth 'full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea' (Isa 11:6-9), the desert blossoming (Isa 35:1-2), and the meek inheriting the land (Ps 37:11). Jesus repeats this when he says the meek 'shall inherit the earth' (Matt 5:5).

Interpreters differ on how literally to take these pictures. Isaiah 65 still mentions death at an old age (Isa 65:20), which suggests to some readers that it describes an improved present age, or a millennium, rather than the final state. Others read it as poetic language for a perfected world.

callout.text: Isaiah 65:20 speaks of someone dying at a hundred being thought young. Premillennialists often see this as describing a millennial kingdom before the final state; amillennialists usually read it as poetic imagery for long, blessed life in the new creation.

sections.heading: The New Testament: groaning creation and a city that comes down
sections.body:
Paul's clearest statement is Romans 8. Creation was 'subjected to futility' but 'will be set free from its bondage to corruption' and share in 'the freedom of the glory of the children of God'. Creation is groaning like a woman in labour, and so are believers, as they wait for 'the redemption of our bodies' (Rom 8:19-23). The fate of the earth is tied to the fate of our bodies: both are to be redeemed, not discarded.

Jesus speaks of 'the renewal of all things' (Matt 19:28, Greek *palingenesia*, 'new birth'). Peter speaks of 'the times of restoration of all things' (Acts 3:21). Paul says God's plan is to unite 'all things in heaven and on earth' in Christ (Eph 1:10) and reconcile 'all things' to himself (Col 1:20).

Revelation's ending is the most vivid. John sees a new heaven and new earth, and the holy city coming *down* out of heaven. The great announcement is 'the dwelling place of God is with man' (Rev 21:1-3). Humans do not go up; God comes down. The final scene includes a river, a tree of life whose leaves are 'for the healing of the nations', and kings bringing their glory into the city (Rev 21:24-26, Rev 22:1-5).

callout.text: Myth: 'The Bible ends with believers in heaven, far away from earth.' Correction: Revelation ends with the heavenly city coming down to a new earth (Rev 21:2-3). Christians disagree about how much continuity there is with this earth, but the final scene is earthly as well as heavenly.

sections.heading: 2 Peter 3: burned up or laid bare?
sections.body:
The strongest 'destruction' text is 2 Peter 3. The heavens will pass away with a roar, the elements will be dissolved with fire, and the earth and its works will be ... what? Older English Bibles (following later Greek manuscripts) say 'burned up'. The oldest Greek manuscripts read a word meaning 'found' or 'exposed', which most modern translations render as 'laid bare' or 'disclosed' (2 Pet 3:10). If 'exposed' is right, the fire is more like a refiner's fire that reveals and judges, not a fire that erases.

The chapter compares this coming fire to the flood: the old world 'perished' in water (2 Pet 3:6), yet the earth was not annihilated; it was cleansed and continued. And the passage ends not with emptiness but with 'new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells' (2 Pet 3:13), echoing Isaiah 65.

Other texts also speak of the heavens 'perishing' and being changed like a garment (Ps 102:25-27, Heb 1:10-12), the earth and sky 'fleeing' (Rev 20:11), and a shaking of everything that can be shaken (Heb 12:26-28). Readers who stress discontinuity take these as signs that the present cosmos will truly end and be replaced. Readers who stress continuity note that the same texts speak of change ('like a garment you will change them'), not simple erasure.

sources.author: Douglas J. Moo
sources.title: Nature in the New Creation: New Testament Eschatology and the Environment
sources.locator: Journal of the Evangelical Theological Society

callout.text: The textual issue in 2 Peter 3:10 is real and well known: the oldest manuscripts (such as Sinaiticus and Vaticanus) read 'will be found', while many later ones read 'will be burned up'. Modern critical editions favour 'found', but translators still disagree on what 'found' means.

sections.heading: Chiliasm: the thousand-year kingdom on earth
sections.body:
In the second century, many Christian leaders expected Christ to reign on a renewed earth for a thousand years before the final judgment, based mainly on Revelation 20:1-6. This view is called chiliasm, from the Greek word for a thousand (*chilioi*).

Papias of Hierapolis (early second century) passed on extravagant pictures of the coming fruitfulness of the earth, including vines with ten thousand branches. Irenaeus preserves these traditions and credits them to 'the elders' who had known John. Justin Martyr says he and other fully orthodox Christians expect a rebuilt Jerusalem and a thousand-year reign, while admitting that many 'pure and devout' Christians think otherwise. Irenaeus defends chiliasm at length at the end of *Against Heresies* (5.32-36). His reason is theological: the righteous must receive their reward in the very creation in which they suffered, and creation itself must be restored to serve them. Tertullian and later Lactantius held similar views.

For these writers, chiliasm was not escapism. It was a strong statement that God's salvation includes the physical world, the land, the city and the harvest.

sources.author: Irenaeus of Lyon
sources.title: Against Heresies
sources.locator: 5.33.3-4 (the elders and Papias on the fruitful vines)

sources.author: Charles E. Hill
sources.title: Regnum Caelorum: Patterns of Millennial Thought in Early Christianity

callout.text: How widespread was chiliasm? Older histories said it was the near-universal view of the second century. Charles E. Hill has argued that non-chiliast views were also common and early, pointing out that Justin himself admits many Christians disagreed. Most scholars now say chiliasm was common and prominent but not universal.

sections.heading: The decline of chiliasm: Origen and Augustine
sections.body:
In the third century, chiliasm came under pressure. Origen of Alexandria mocked those who expected bodily pleasures in the kingdom and read the promises spiritually, as pointing to the soul's ascent to God. Around 250, Bishop Dionysius of Alexandria debated the followers of an Egyptian bishop, Nepos, who taught a literal millennium, and he also raised doubts about whether the apostle John wrote Revelation. Eusebius, the church historian, called Papias 'a man of very little intelligence' for his literalism.

In the West, Augustine of Hippo (City of God, book 20) admits he once held a form of chiliasm. He then gave the reading that shaped Western Christianity for a thousand years: the 'thousand years' of Revelation 20 is the whole period of the church, from Christ's first coming to his return, during which Satan is bound and the saints reign with Christ. This became what is now called amillennialism.

The result was a more spiritual and church-centred future hope. The resurrection of the body remained official doctrine, and many theologians, including Augustine and Aquinas, still taught that the physical world would be renewed rather than destroyed. But the emotional centre of hope moved towards heaven and the vision of God.

sources.author: Augustine of Hippo
sources.title: City of God
sources.locator: 20.16 (the world's form changed by fire, not its substance destroyed)

callout.text: Myth: 'Chiliasm was condemned as a heresy by an early ecumenical council.' Correction: no early ecumenical council formally condemned chiliasm. The phrase 'whose kingdom shall have no end' in the Creed of 381 is usually linked to the teaching of Marcellus of Ancyra, not to millennialism. Chiliasm declined mainly through theological argument and changing tastes.

sections.heading: Medieval and later piety: 'going to heaven'
sections.body:
Through the Middle Ages, official teaching kept the resurrection of the body and a renewed world. Thomas Aquinas, for example, discussed how the physical world would be renewed after the judgment. Caroline Walker Bynum has shown how intensely medieval thinkers cared about the body's resurrection, down to the question of how scattered remains would be reassembled.

Yet the centre of everyday hope shifted. The vision of God (the 'beatific vision') in heaven became the main picture of final happiness, defined for Catholics in 1336 as something the saints enjoy even before the resurrection. Dante's *Paradiso* pictures the blessed in heavenly spheres of light. Many later hymns, revival songs and sermons, Protestant as well as Catholic, spoke of heaven as a faraway home and the earth as a place to pass through. Some Lutheran theologians of the seventeenth century (for example Johann Gerhard) taught that the present world would be annihilated, not renewed.

Historians debate how to describe this. Some speak of a 'loss' of biblical hope. Others say the emphasis on heaven was a faithful development of texts like Philippians 1:23 and Colossians 3:1-4, and that earthly renewal was never denied, only less often preached.

sources.author: Caroline Walker Bynum
sources.title: The Resurrection of the Body in Western Christianity, 200-1336

sources.author: Thomas Aquinas (completed by his students)
sources.title: Summa Theologiae, Supplement
sources.locator: q. 91 (the state of the world after the judgment)

sources.author: Johann Gerhard
sources.title: Loci Theologici
sources.locator: locus on the consummation of the world

sections.heading: The modern recovery of new creation
sections.body:
In the twentieth century, biblical scholars began stressing again that Jewish and early Christian hope was earthy and bodily. Abraham Kuyper and later Dutch Reformed writers spoke of creation being restored rather than replaced. Jürgen Moltmann put the hope of new creation at the centre of his *Theology of Hope* (1964).

Among popular writers, N. T. Wright's *Surprised by Hope* (2008) argued that 'going to heaven when you die' is not the Christian hope; it is, as he put it, 'life after life after death': a time with Christ after death, followed by bodily resurrection in a renewed creation. J. Richard Middleton's *A New Heaven and a New Earth* (2014) argued the whole Bible, from Genesis to Revelation, points to a holistic, this-worldly renewal. Others have linked this to care for the environment, work and culture, since what we do on earth may have lasting value (1 Cor 15:58).

This emphasis now has wide support across evangelical, Catholic and Orthodox scholarship. The Catholic Catechism, for example, speaks of the visible universe being transformed so that it can serve the righteous.

sources.author: J. Richard Middleton
sources.title: A New Heaven and a New Earth: Reclaiming Biblical Eschatology

sections.heading: Critiques of the new-creation emphasis
sections.body:
Not everyone is persuaded. Michael Allen's *Grounded in Heaven* (2018) and Hans Boersma's *Seeing God* (2018) argue that some new-creation writing has become too focused on creation and too little on God himself. The deepest hope, they say, is not a renewed earth but seeing God face to face (Matt 5:8, 1 John 3:2, Rev 22:4), and older 'heavenly-minded' piety rightly saw that.

Other critics say the contrast between 'Platonic' tradition and 'biblical' new creation is overdrawn: Augustine and Aquinas already taught bodily resurrection and cosmic renewal, so the recovery is less of a rediscovery than it sounds. Some worry that new-creation language can drift into a social programme, as if humans build the kingdom, whereas scripture presents the new creation as God's gift (Rev 21:2, 2 Pet 3:13). And some dispensationalist and other readers hold that 2 Peter 3 and Revelation 20:11 point to a real end of the present cosmos and a fresh creation.

New-creation writers reply that seeing God and living in a renewed world are not rivals: in Revelation the vision of God's face takes place in the city on the new earth (Rev 22:3-5). Many on both sides now agree on that combination, while still disagreeing on emphasis.

title: The Restoration of All Things
question: What does the Bible mean by the 'restoration of all things', and does it mean that everyone will finally be saved?
plainAnswer: In Acts 3:21 Peter says Jesus must stay in heaven 'until the times of restoration of all things' that God spoke about through the prophets. The Greek word for restoration, *apokatastasis*, became famous because some early theologians, especially Origen and Gregory of Nyssa, used it for the hope that every person (and perhaps even the devil) would finally be reconciled to God. But the word itself is broad. In context it can mean the restoration of Israel and God's kingdom, or the renewal of the whole creation, without saying anything about every individual. Christians have read the related verses in all three ways, and the universalist reading has strong modern defenders and strong traditional objections. Whether the church formally condemned universalism in 543 and 553 is itself debated by historians.
keyTakeaways: *Apokatastasis* simply means 'restoration'; the word alone does not settle who or what is restored.
In Acts, the nearest context is the restoration of Israel and the kingdom (Acts 1:6, Acts 3:19-21).
Texts like Colossians 1:20, Ephesians 1:10 and 1 Corinthians 15:28 speak of God reconciling or uniting 'all things', which many read as cosmic renewal.
Origen, Gregory of Nyssa and Isaac the Syrian hoped for the restoration of all persons; modern defenders include David Bentley Hart, Thomas Talbott and Robin Parry.
Traditional objections point to texts about final, eternal judgment and to the role of human freedom.
Justinian's edict of 543 and the anathemas linked to the council of 553 condemned an Origenist system, but whether they bind the church against every form of universal hope is disputed.

sections.heading: The word: what apokatastasis means
sections.body:
The Greek noun *apokatastasis* and its verb *apokathistēmi* mean 'to restore' or 'put back into a former state'. In ordinary Greek they were used for healing a limb, returning property, or the planets returning to an earlier position.

The Gospels use the verb for healing: a withered hand is 'restored' (Mark 3:5). The Greek Old Testament uses it in Malachi's promise that Elijah will 'restore' the hearts of fathers to their children (Mal 4:5-6), which Jesus echoes when he says Elijah comes and 'will restore all things' (Matt 17:11). The disciples ask the risen Jesus whether he will now 'restore the kingdom to Israel' (Acts 1:6).

So the word is about restoration in general. What is being restored, and to what, has to be learned from the context each time.

callout.text: Myth: 'The word apokatastasis in Acts 3:21 proves universal salvation.' Correction: the word simply means restoration. Universalists build their case on several texts and theological arguments, not on this word alone, and most universalist scholars admit Acts 3:21 is not decisive by itself.

sections.heading: Acts 3:21 in context
sections.body:
Peter is speaking to a Jewish crowd in the temple after healing a lame man. He calls them to repent 'that times of refreshing may come', so that God may send the Messiah, 'whom heaven must receive until the times of restoration of all things which God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets' (Acts 3:19-21).

Two details matter. First, the 'all things' are qualified by 'which God spoke by the prophets'. Some grammarians read this as 'the restoration of all the things the prophets promised', limiting the scope to what was prophesied. Others say the prophets themselves promised a cosmic renewal, so the scope is still very wide. Second, the setting echoes the disciples' question about restoring the kingdom to Israel (Acts 1:6). Many commentators therefore read Acts 3:21 first of all as the fulfilment of Israel's hopes: the return of the Messiah, the renewal of God's people and the blessing of all nations through Abraham's seed (Acts 3:25-26).

The same sermon also warns that anyone who will not listen to the prophet like Moses 'shall be destroyed from among the people' (Acts 3:23). Traditional readers think this rules out a universalist reading here; universalist readers reply that warnings of judgment and a final restoration can both be true if judgment is not the last word.

sections.heading: The related 'all things' texts
sections.body:
Several of Paul's letters use 'all' language about the end. God's plan is 'to unite all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth' (Eph 1:10). Through Christ God was pleased 'to reconcile to himself all things, whether on earth or in heaven, making peace by the blood of his cross' (Col 1:20). At the end Christ hands the kingdom to the Father 'that God may be all in all' (1 Cor 15:24-28). God 'has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all' (Rom 11:32). Every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Phil 2:10-11). Paul also writes, 'as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive' (1 Cor 15:22), and 'one act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all men' (Rom 5:18).

These texts are the heart of the debate. They can be read as: (1) God restoring his creation and his people as a whole; (2) God pacifying all hostile powers, bringing everything under Christ's rule, whether willingly or not; or (3) God actually reconciling every person, so that every bended knee is a glad one.

Context matters for each. Romans 11:32 comes at the end of a discussion of Jews and Gentiles as groups. Philippians 2:10-11 quotes Isaiah 45:23, where the bowing includes those who were 'incensed' against God and are 'put to shame' (Isa 45:24). Colossians 1:20 is followed by a condition: 'if indeed you continue in the faith' (Col 1:23). Universalist readers answer that the same 'all' is used on both sides of Adam and Christ (1 Cor 15:22, Rom 5:18), and that 'confess' in scripture is usually the language of praise, not forced surrender.

sections.heading: Reading 1: the restoration of Israel and the kingdom
sections.body:
On this reading, 'restoration' is about God keeping his promises to Israel. The prophets foresaw the return of the scattered tribes, a renewed covenant, a restored Jerusalem and the nations streaming to worship (Jer 31:31-34, Isa 2:2-4, Amos 9:11-12). Jesus chooses twelve apostles who will 'sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel' at 'the renewal' (Matt 19:28). Acts 15 quotes Amos about rebuilding David's fallen tent as Gentiles join God's people (Acts 15:16-17).

Different traditions fill this in differently. Dispensational and many Messianic Jewish readers expect a future national restoration of Israel in the land. Others (much Reformed and Catholic interpretation) see the restoration fulfilled in Christ and the church, Jew and Gentile together, with perhaps a future large-scale turning of Jewish people to Christ (Rom 11:25-27). Either way, the focus is on God's people and kingdom, not on each individual human.

callout.text: How Israel's restoration is fulfilled is itself a major debate (see the Israel and the Church debate). Scholars agree that Acts 1:6 and 3:21 are about Israel's hope; they disagree about whether that hope is fulfilled mainly in the church or still awaits a national fulfilment.

sections.heading: Reading 2: the renewal of creation
sections.body:
On this reading, the restoration of all things is the healing of the whole created order: the 'renewal of all things' (Matt 19:28), creation set free from decay (Rom 8:19-23), and the new heaven and new earth (Rev 21:1-5). 'All things' in Colossians 1:20 and Ephesians 1:10 includes 'things in heaven and on earth', the whole cosmos, not just people.

This was a major theme for Irenaeus, who spoke of creation being restored to its original state and made to serve the righteous. It is common today in Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant theology. It is compatible with believing in a final judgment in which some are lost, because what is restored is creation as such, purified of evil, not necessarily every individual within it. Revelation, for example, describes a renewed city with some still 'outside' (Rev 22:14-15).

Critics from the universalist side ask whether a creation can be truly 'restored' and God truly 'all in all' while some of his creatures remain forever in rebellion or torment. Defenders reply that God being all in all can include just judgment, and that evil is defeated even if not every evildoer is reconciled.

sources.author: J. Richard Middleton
sources.title: A New Heaven and a New Earth

sections.heading: Reading 3: universal reconciliation of all persons
sections.body:
On this reading, God will in the end bring every person into loving union with himself, through and after judgment. Punishment is real and may be long and severe, but it is remedial, like a refiner's fire (Mal 3:2-3, 1 Cor 3:13-15), not endless.

Clement of Alexandria described divine punishment as corrective. Origen (died about 253) taught that all rational beings, having fallen, would through long ages of education and purification return to God; whether he included the devil was disputed even in his lifetime. Gregory of Nyssa, a revered fourth-century bishop and defender of the Nicene Creed, taught that evil is finite and will be emptied out, so that in the end God will be 'all in all' with no one left outside (*On the Soul and the Resurrection*, *Catechetical Oration* 26). Isaac the Syrian, a seventh-century bishop and monk loved in Eastern spirituality, wrote that the 'scourge of love' in Gehenna serves God's purpose of mercy and expressed hope for the final good of all. Augustine noted that in his day many Christians, whom he called 'the merciful', hoped for an end to punishment, and he argued against them.

Modern defenders include Thomas Talbott (*The Inescapable Love of God*), Robin Parry (*The Evangelical Universalist*, first published under the pen name Gregory MacDonald) and David Bentley Hart (*That All Shall Be Saved*). Their main arguments are: the 'all' texts above; God's character as perfect love who 'desires all people to be saved' (1 Tim 2:4); the claim that a free creature fully seeing the truth could not forever reject the Good; and the moral difficulty of endless punishment for finite sins. Some Christians, such as Hans Urs von Balthasar, stop short of universalism and speak instead of a legitimate hope that all may be saved.

callout.text: Myth: 'Christian universalists deny hell and judgment.' Correction: most Christian universalists affirm that hell is real and that sin will be judged, sometimes severely and for long ages. What they deny is that it is endless or that it is God's final word for anyone.

sections.heading: The traditional objections
sections.body:
Most of the church, East and West, has held that some will finally be lost. Their main objections to universal restoration are these.

Explicit texts of final judgment. Jesus contrasts 'eternal punishment' with 'eternal life' using the same adjective (Matt 25:46). He speaks of a sin that will not be forgiven 'in this age or in the age to come' (Matt 12:32), of the unquenchable fire (Mark 9:43-48), and of Judas, that it would have been better for him not to have been born (Mark 14:21). Paul speaks of 'eternal destruction' away from the Lord's presence (2 Thess 1:9). Revelation describes a lake of fire with no hint of exit (Rev 20:10, Rev 20:14-15).

Context of the 'all' texts. Critics argue that Paul's 'all' often means 'all kinds' (Jews and Gentiles) or 'all who are in Christ' (1 Cor 15:22-23 goes on, 'those who belong to Christ'), and that the cosmic reconciliation of Colossians 1:20 can mean the subduing of enemies, not their conversion (Col 2:15).

Freedom and love. If God's love respects human freedom, some may freely and finally refuse it; C. S. Lewis put it that the doors of hell are 'locked on the inside'. Urgency. Critics worry universalism weakens the call to repent and to mission (Heb 9:27, 2 Cor 6:2).

Universalists reply that *aiōnios* can mean 'of the age to come' rather than 'endless' (see 'Heaven and Hell Explained'); that 'not in this age or the age to come' speaks of these ages, not of all eternity; that true freedom is oriented to the good; and that the early universalists were fervent preachers of repentance.

sources.author: Michael J. McClymond
sources.title: The Devil's Redemption: A New History and Interpretation of Christian Universalism

sections.heading: The 543 and 553 question
sections.body:
In 543 the emperor Justinian issued an edict against Origen's teachings, with a list of anathemas (formal condemnations), approved by a local synod in Constantinople. One condemned the idea that the punishment of demons and wicked people is temporary and will end in a restoration. In 553 the Second Council of Constantinople, the fifth ecumenical council, met mainly to deal with a different controversy (the 'Three Chapters'). Its canon 11 lists Origen among heretics. A separate set of fifteen anathemas against Origenist teachings, beginning with the pre-existence of souls and 'the monstrous restoration that follows from it', is associated with the council.

Historians debate what this settled. Points in dispute include: whether the fifteen anathemas were formally approved by the ecumenical council or only by bishops gathered just before it opened; whether Origen's name in canon 11 was original; and whether the condemnations target universal salvation as such or a specific sixth-century Origenist system (pre-existent minds, a return to pure spirit, spherical resurrection bodies) linked with Evagrius. Notably, Gregory of Nyssa, who taught universal restoration without pre-existence, was never condemned and is venerated as a saint.

Scholars such as Ilaria Ramelli argue that the church never condemned universal hope as such. Scholars such as Brian Daley and Michael McClymond hold that, whatever the procedural details, the church received these condemnations as rejecting Origenist universalism, and that the later tradition overwhelmingly treated endless punishment as church teaching. Readers should treat the precise binding force of 553 as an open historical question.

title: Heaven and Hell Explained
question: What does the Bible actually say about heaven and hell, and what are the main Christian views?
plainAnswer: The Bible uses several different words that English Bibles often flatten into 'hell': Sheol and Hades (the realm of the dead), Gehenna (a place of final judgment named after a valley outside Jerusalem), Tartarus (a prison for rebel angels) and the lake of fire. Christians agree that God will judge evil and that the outcome is serious, but they hold three main views of what final judgment means: endless conscious punishment, final destruction of the wicked (conditional immortality), or a punishment that finally leads everyone to God (Christian universalism). On heaven, some stress going to be with God in heaven, while others stress that the final goal is resurrection on a renewed earth; many hold both, in two stages. Each view has serious biblical arguments, real weaknesses and thoughtful defenders.
keyTakeaways: 'Hell' in English Bibles translates several different words with different meanings; reading them carefully prevents a lot of confusion.
Sheol and Hades usually mean the realm of the dead, not the place of final punishment.
Eternal conscious torment has been the majority view in church history; conditional immortality and universalism both have early roots and serious modern defenders.
Much of the debate turns on a few words: 'eternal' (aiōnios), 'destroy', 'death', 'all'.
Each view is regularly caricatured; the strongest versions are more careful than their critics often allow.
On heaven, the biggest divide is about emphasis: going to God in heaven, or God coming to a renewed earth; most traditions affirm both in sequence.

sections.heading: Sheol and Hades: the realm of the dead
sections.body:
In the Old Testament, the dead go down to Sheol. It is pictured as a dark, silent place under the earth where both good and bad people go (Gen 37:35, Eccl 9:10). The psalmists worry that in Sheol no one praises God (Ps 6:5, Ps 88:10-12), but they also hope God will not abandon them there (Ps 16:10, Ps 49:15). Older translations such as the King James Version sometimes render Sheol as 'hell', which misleads modern readers into thinking of a place of punishment.

The Greek Old Testament translated Sheol as Hades, and the New Testament uses Hades the same way: the realm of the dead. Jesus says the gates of Hades will not overcome his church (Matt 16:18); Peter says Jesus was not abandoned to Hades (Acts 2:27); the risen Christ holds 'the keys of Death and Hades' (Rev 1:18). In the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, Hades has a place of torment and a place of comfort (Luke 16:23). At the end, Death and Hades themselves are thrown into the lake of fire (Rev 20:13-14), which shows that Hades is temporary.

In short, Sheol and Hades mostly describe where the dead are now, not the final destiny.

callout.text: Myth: 'Every time the Bible says hell it means the place of eternal fire.' Correction: many older 'hell' passages translate Sheol or Hades, the realm of all the dead. Jacob expects to go to Sheol mourning his son (Gen 37:35); that is not a fear of damnation.

sections.heading: Gehenna, Tartarus and the lake of fire
sections.body:
Gehenna is the word Jesus uses most for final judgment (Matt 5:22, Matt 10:28, Mark 9:43-48). It comes from the Valley of Hinnom on the south side of Jerusalem, where some kings of Judah had sacrificed children by fire (2 Kgs 23:10, Jer 7:31-32). Jeremiah prophesied it would become a 'valley of slaughter' full of corpses. By Jesus' time, Jewish writings used Gehenna as the name for the place of punishment after judgment. Jesus describes it with fire that is not quenched and the worm that does not die, quoting the last verse of Isaiah (Mark 9:48, Isa 66:24).

Tartarus appears once, as a verb: God 'cast them into Tartarus' about angels who sinned, holding them in chains of darkness until the judgment (2 Pet 2:4). In Greek myth Tartarus was the deepest prison of the underworld. Peter borrows the word for the holding place of fallen angels, not human beings.

The lake of fire appears only in Revelation. The beast and false prophet are thrown into it, then the devil, then Death and Hades, and then anyone not found in the book of life (Rev 19:20, Rev 20:10, Rev 20:14-15). Revelation calls it 'the second death' (Rev 20:14, Rev 21:8). How literally to take its fire, and what 'second death' implies, is part of the debate below.

callout.text: Myth: 'Gehenna was Jerusalem's burning rubbish dump, and Jesus just meant the town dump.' Correction: there is no ancient evidence for a perpetually burning dump in the Hinnom valley. The idea is usually traced to the medieval Jewish commentator David Kimhi (around 1200). Gehenna's power came from its history of child sacrifice and Jeremiah's prophecy of judgment, and by Jesus' day it was already a name for final punishment.

sections.heading: What does 'eternal' (aionios) mean?
sections.body:
The Greek adjective *aiōnios* comes from *aiōn*, 'age'. It appears in 'eternal life' and also in 'eternal punishment', 'eternal fire' and 'eternal destruction' (Matt 25:46, Jude 1:7, 2 Thess 1:9). How it is understood shapes each view.

Traditional readers note that in Matthew 25:46 the same word describes life and punishment side by side, so if the life is endless the punishment must be too. Conditionalists usually agree that *aiōnios* means everlasting but argue it often describes the result, not an ongoing process: 'eternal destruction' is a destruction whose result lasts forever, just as 'eternal redemption' (Heb 9:12) is a redemption done once with permanent effects. Universalists, following scholars such as Ilaria Ramelli and David Konstan, argue that *aiōnios* in Jewish and Christian Greek often means 'belonging to the age to come' rather than strictly 'endless', so 'eternal punishment' could mean 'the punishment of the coming age', with its duration left open.

The word alone cannot settle the debate. Each side must also explain the wider context and other texts. Readers should notice which meaning a translation or teacher is assuming.

sources.author: Ilaria L. E. Ramelli and David Konstan
sources.title: Terms for Eternity: Aiônios and Aïdios in Classical and Christian Texts

sections.heading: View 1: Eternal conscious torment
sections.body:
What it says: those who die unrepentant will exist forever under God's just judgment, consciously experiencing loss and punishment, cut off from the joy of God's presence. Many defenders today stress that the core of hell is separation from God and the self-chosen ruin of a life turned away from him, while still taking the fire imagery seriously. This is the historic majority view of Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches, taught by Augustine, Aquinas, Luther, Calvin and Jonathan Edwards, and stated in confessions such as the Athanasian Creed and the Westminster Confession.

Main arguments: Jesus places 'eternal punishment' alongside 'eternal life' (Matt 25:46). Revelation says the smoke of torment 'goes up forever and ever' and the devil, beast and false prophet are 'tormented day and night forever and ever' (Rev 14:10-11, Rev 20:10). Jesus speaks of an undying worm and unquenchable fire (Mark 9:48). Sin against an infinitely holy God is infinitely serious, and the wicked may continue to sin and refuse God forever.

Critiques: an endless punishment for sins done in a finite life seems disproportionate; Revelation 20:10 names the devil, beast and false prophet, not humans in general; and the 'forever' smoke echoes Old Testament images for a city destroyed once and for all (Isa 34:9-10). Replies: the seriousness of sin depends on whom it is against, not how long it took; Revelation 14:11 does concern humans who worship the beast; and the human and devilish fates share the same lake of fire (Matt 25:41).

sources.author: Christopher W. Morgan and Robert A. Peterson (eds.)
sources.title: Hell Under Fire

sources.author: Denny Burk
sources.title: Eternal Conscious Torment, in Four Views on Hell (ed. Preston Sprinkle), 2nd edition

callout.text: Straw man: 'Believers in eternal torment think God enjoys torturing people.' Correction: its serious defenders say God takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezek 33:11), that hell is the just consequence of refusing God, and that its worst aspect is loss of God, not a torture chamber run by demons.

sections.heading: View 2: Conditional immortality (annihilationism)
sections.body:
What it says: humans are not immortal by nature; eternal life is God's gift given in Christ. The unrepentant will be raised, judged and punished in proportion to their sins, and then will finally cease to exist: the 'second death'. Defenders often call it 'conditional immortality' because immortality is conditional on union with Christ. Early writers such as Justin (on one reading), Theophilus and Arnobius are cited for it. Modern defenders include Edward Fudge, John Stott (cautiously, in *Essentials*, 1988), Clark Pinnock, John Stackhouse and the Rethinking Hell project.

Main arguments: only God 'has immortality' (1 Tim 6:16) and believers 'seek' it (Rom 2:7); the Bible's most common words for the fate of the wicked are death, destruction and perishing (John 3:16, Rom 6:23, Matt 10:28, Phil 3:19); God can 'destroy both soul and body in Gehenna' (Matt 10:28); the wicked become ashes and are 'no more' (Mal 4:1-3, Ps 37:10, Ps 37:20); Sodom's 'eternal fire' destroyed the cities, it did not keep burning (Jude 1:7, 2 Pet 2:6). The unquenchable fire and undying worm of Isaiah 66:24 consume corpses, not living people.

Critiques: it seems to weaken the 'eternal punishment' contrast of Matthew 25:46; Revelation 14:11 and 20:10 speak of torment with 'no rest day or night'; and the view has sometimes been linked to groups outside historic orthodoxy. Replies: the punishment is eternal in its result, as 'eternal destruction' (2 Thess 1:9) shows; Revelation's imagery is symbolic, drawing on Isaiah 34; and the view is now held by many orthodox evangelicals and has early patristic precedent.

sources.title: Essentials: A Liberal-Evangelical Dialogue

sources.author: Christopher M. Date, Gregory G. Stump and Joshua W. Anderson (eds.)
sources.title: Rethinking Hell: Readings in Evangelical Conditionalism

callout.text: Straw man: 'Annihilationists believe the wicked just die and get off lightly, with no judgment.' Correction: conditionalists teach a real resurrection to judgment and punishment proportionate to sin before final destruction. They see permanent loss of existence and of God as the ultimate penalty, not an escape.

sections.heading: View 3: Christian universalism (restorationism)
sections.body:
What it says: God will finally reconcile every person to himself through Christ. Hell is real, but it is a purifying, corrective fire, not endless; people may suffer long and severely, but no one is beyond God's love forever. Early defenders include Origen and Gregory of Nyssa, and Isaac the Syrian expressed a similar hope. Modern defenders include Thomas Talbott, Robin Parry and David Bentley Hart. It is distinct from pluralism, the idea that all religions are equally valid; Christian universalists hold that everyone is saved through Christ.

Main arguments: God 'desires all people to be saved' (1 Tim 2:4) and is 'the Saviour of all people, especially of those who believe' (1 Tim 4:10); 'as in Adam all die, so in Christ shall all be made alive' (1 Cor 15:22); God will reconcile all things (Col 1:20) and be 'all in all' (1 Cor 15:28); every tongue will confess Jesus as Lord (Phil 2:10-11); the gates of the new Jerusalem are never shut (Rev 21:25); God does not cast off forever (Lam 3:31-33). Philosophically, they argue that a perfectly loving and all-powerful God would not allow any creature to be lost forever, and that endless punishment serves no good end.

Critiques: it seems to contradict texts of final, unending judgment (Matt 25:46, 2 Thess 1:9); it may override human freedom; it was condemned in 543 and 553 (see 'The Restoration of All Things'); and it risks removing urgency from the call to repent. Replies: universalists read *aiōnios* as 'of the age to come'; they argue freedom is fulfilled, not overridden, when people see God clearly; they dispute the scope of the sixth-century condemnations; and they point out that Gregory of Nyssa and others preached repentance fervently.

sources.author: David Bentley Hart
sources.title: That All Shall Be Saved: Heaven, Hell, and Universal Salvation

callout.text: Straw man: 'Universalists think sin does not matter and everyone goes straight to heaven.' Correction: Christian universalists usually hold that sin is grievous, that judgment is real and may be terrible, and that salvation comes only through Christ. They differ on whether judgment ends in restoration.

sections.heading: Heaven: destination or new creation?
sections.body:
Christians agree that the final hope is to be with God in perfect joy. They differ in how they describe it.

The 'heaven as destination' emphasis focuses on the vision of God: the pure in heart 'shall see God' (Matt 5:8), 'we shall see him as he is' (1 John 3:2), 'now face to face' (1 Cor 13:12). Believers have an inheritance 'kept in heaven' (1 Pet 1:4), a 'better country, that is, a heavenly one' (Heb 11:16), and rooms in the Father's house (John 14:2-3). This picture shaped classic Catholic and Protestant teaching on the beatific vision.

The 'new creation' emphasis focuses on bodily resurrection and a renewed world: creation set free (Rom 8:19-23), new heavens and new earth (Isa 65:17, 2 Pet 3:13), and the holy city coming down so that God dwells with people (Rev 21:1-3). Heaven, on this view, is where God's future is kept now, before it comes to earth (Col 3:1-4, Phil 3:20-21).

Most traditions combine these in two stages: at death believers go to be with Christ (Phil 1:23, Luke 23:43, 2 Cor 5:8), the 'intermediate state'; at Christ's return they are raised bodily for life in the new creation, where they see God face to face (Rev 22:3-5). The disagreement is often about which part to emphasise in preaching and hope.

sources.author: Hans Boersma
sources.title: Seeing God: The Beatific Vision in Christian Tradition

callout.text: Myth: 'Heaven is sitting on clouds playing harps forever.' Correction: harps appear in Revelation's worship scenes (Rev 5:8), but the Bible's final picture is a city, a garden, a river, nations, work and worship on a renewed earth, centred on God's presence. The 'clouds and harps' picture comes mainly from art and cartoons.

sections.heading: Common straw men to avoid
sections.body:
Because hell is an emotional subject, each view is often attacked in a weak form.

About hell in general: 'Satan rules hell and tortures people.' Scripture pictures the devil as a prisoner thrown into the lake of fire, not its king (Rev 20:10, Matt 25:41). The image of Satan as ruler of hell comes largely from later literature and art.

About the debate itself: 'Only liberals question eternal torment.' In fact, conditional immortality and universalism both have early Christian defenders, and conditionalism in particular is now held by many theologically conservative evangelicals. On the other side, 'only harsh fundamentalists believe in eternal torment' is also false; it has been the view of most of the church's most compassionate saints and thinkers.

About Jesus: 'Jesus never talked about hell; Paul invented it' and 'Paul talked about hell constantly' are both wrong. Most of the New Testament's Gehenna sayings come from Jesus (Matt 5:29-30, Matt 23:33). Paul speaks of wrath, death and destruction (Rom 2:5-8, 2 Thess 1:9) but never uses the word Gehenna.

A fair discussion names the strongest texts on every side and admits that each view has passages it must work hard to explain.

callout.text: The biggest denominations officially teach eternal punishment (for example Catechism of the Catholic Church 1033-1037), but many emphasise the hell of self-exclusion from God more than physical fire. The Church of England's Doctrine Commission report *The Mystery of Salvation* (1995) described hell in terms of final non-being, showing the range within one church (needs verification of exact wording).

views.name: Eternal conscious torment
views.summary: The unrepentant exist forever under just judgment and separation from God. Historic majority view (Augustine, Aquinas, Calvin, Edwards).

views.name: Conditional immortality
views.summary: Immortality is God's gift; the unrepentant are punished and then finally destroyed. Held by Fudge, Stott (tentatively), Stackhouse and others.

views.name: Christian universalism
views.summary: Judgment is real but remedial; God finally reconciles everyone through Christ. Held by Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, and today by Talbott, Parry and Hart.

views.name: Heaven as destination
views.summary: The final goal is the vision of God in heaven.

views.name: New creation
views.summary: The final goal is bodily resurrection on a renewed earth where God dwells with his people.

furtherQuestions: Which of the 'hell' words in your own Bible translation are Sheol, Hades, Gehenna or Tartarus?
Does the same word 'eternal' in Matthew 25:46 have to mean the same thing for life and for punishment?
Is the fire of Gehenna best read literally, symbolically, or both?
How do each view's supporters handle the texts that seem to favour the others?
If heaven is finally on a renewed earth, how should that change how we speak at funerals?
